title: Sub-Tenon’s, Peribulbar & Intravitreal Injection Protocols
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to posterior segment drug delivery via sub-Tenon’s, peribulbar, and intravitreal routes. Includes procedural steps, medication dosages, and RCOphth guidelines for ocular therapeutics.

sections.title: Ocular Injection Routes & Applications
sections.content: In addition to their use in ocular anaesthesia (see E Ocular anaesthesia, pp. 1040–1 to pp. 1044–5), the sub-Tenon’s and peribulbar routes may be used to deliver drugs, such as corticosteroids, to the posterior aspect of the globe. Although primarily used for ocular anaesthesia (e.g. lidocaine, bupivacaine), these routes may be used for delivering corticosteroids (e.g. triamcinolone, methylprednisolone) in posterior segment inflammation, exudation, or macular oedema.

sections.title: Sub-Tenon’s Cannula Technique (Box 25.1)
content: 1. Apply Topical anaesthetic to conjunctiva (e.g. proxymetacaine 0.5%).
2. Wash hands, and don sterile gloves.
3. Instil 5% povidone iodine onto the ocular surface; drape (optional), and insert lid speculum (optional).
4. Ask patient to look in opposite direction to intended injection site (e.g. inferonasally).
5. Open conjunctiva around 8mm from the limbus (e.g. superotemporally).
6. Dissect down to bare sclera with blunt curved scissors.
7. Insert sub-Tenon’s cannula (19G, 25mm, blunt, curved), and slide posteriorly along the globe.
8. Inject medication.
9. Carefully withdraw cannula; forceps or a cotton-tipped applicator can be used to provide countertraction and to hold the conjunctival opening closed (which may help reduce regurgitation).

rows: Relatively safe (blunt needle, appropriately curved for globe shape).
Significant regurgitation along track may result in poor drug delivery.
Less regurgitation and improved drug delivery.
Relatively safe (blunt, flexible, moulds to globe). Less regurgitation than Sub-Tenon's cannula.
Can be difficult to direct the flexible cannula.

sections.title: Step-by-Step: IV Cannula Technique
content: Enter sub-Tenon’s space using the trocar of a 22G or 23G, 0.9/25mm PTFE IV cannula.
Advance cannula (trocar engaged, bevel-up) for about 3mm within space.
Slightly withdraw trocar (sharp end no longer exposed); advance cannula further 3mm.
Completely withdraw trocar.
Direct cannula posteriorly for further 12–15mm using gentle rotatory movements.
Attach syringe to cannula and inject medication.

sections.title: Peribulbar Injection Protocol
content: Definition: Sharp needle technique for extraconal space delivery.
Anesthesia preference: Medial compartment block via medial canthal injection (p. 930).
Safety Note: For corticosteroids, the safer sub-Tenon’s route is recommended.
Method: Inferolateral injection using 25G sharp-bevel needle.
Entry: Through lid or conjunctiva.
Direction: Inferolateral to globe, just above orbital floor.

sections.title: Corticosteroid Licensing Notes
sections.content: These are non-licensed uses of commercial IM/intra-articular preparations. Kenalog® is preserved with benzyl alcohol and is not licensed for intraocular use. Triesence® and Trivaris® are preservative-free and licensed for intravitreal use (UK via importers). *Depo-Medrone contains polyethylene glycol and myristyl-γ-picolinium chloride.

branches: Principles: Isotonic, neutral pH, no preservatives
Vascular/Exudative: Anti-VEGF or Corticosteroids for AMD, CMO, etc.
Setting: Theatre or dedicated clean room (enclosed, free from interruptions, good illumination, washable floor, non-particulate ceiling)

sections.title: Intravitreal Procedure: Preparation
content: Confirm consent and correct eye.
Measure IOP.
Ensure adequate dilation.
Instil topical anaesthesia.
Set up trolley; ensure all treatments (including post-injection antibiotics) are available.
Hands washed and sterile gloves worn (Full gowning not necessary).

sections.title: Intravitreal Technique (RCOphth Guidelines)
content: 1. Wash hands, don sterile gloves.
2. 5% Povidone iodine to ocular surface (allow 3min).
3. Clean periocular area with 5–10% povidone iodine.
4. Drape and insert lid speculum.
5. Consider supplemental anaesthesia (subconjunctival/sub-Tenon’s lidocaine 1%).
6. Prepare syringe immediately; expel air; maintain asepsis.
7. Identify site: Inferotemporal quadrant (Avoid horizontal meridians).
8. Site Distance: 3.0–3.5mm (aphakic/pseudophakic) or 3.5–4mm (phakic) from limbus.
9. Insert needle (27–30G; 1/2–5/8in) perpendicularly toward globe centre.
10. Inject therapeutic agent (Max 0.1mL).
11. Remove needle; use sterile cotton-tip for counterpressure/reflux prevention.

sections.title: Critical Post-Injection Care
content: Test gross VA and check central retinal artery patency.
URGENT: If non-perfusion occurs (often no perception of light), perform AC paracentesis immediately.
Check injection site at slit-lamp and IOP (not mandatory).
Topical antibiotics (e.g. chloramphenicol 0.5% 4x/d for ≥3d) are at clinician discretion.
RCOphth & SPC (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept) Note: Routine post-injection antibiotics are not recommended due to lack of evidence.

sections.title: Corticosteroid Footnotes (NICE & Licensing)
sections.content:
* Dexamethasone (Ozurdex®): NICE-approved for macular oedema post-RVO (TA229), DMO (TA349), and non-infectious posterior uveitis in adults (ID763).
† Fluocinolone (Iluvien®): NICE-approved for DMO insufficiently responsive to other therapies in pseudophakic patients (TA301).
‡ Triamcinolone: Kenalog® contains benzyl alcohol (not licensed for intraocular use). Triesence® and Trivaris® are alcohol-free and licensed for intravitreal use.
